summary: Independent review of jinshu/072 completed. All 27 owned items (15 claims + 12 hints) and all 12 owned people were checked against source units s0002–s0057. Three checks were corrected in response to host feedback: (1) claim-24's reason was fixed from a reversed 317–316 interval to the correct 317–322 AD, matching the sealed item's exact value; (2) claim-22's reason was expanded to justify the 290–313 AD event-uncertainty window from 惠懷之際 as a period of turmoil rather than a simple import of two reigns; (3) claim-54's reason was strengthened to establish that 終於建平太守 is the classical biographical formula for death in office, not merely the last office held. All other checks remain supported by the Chinese source text. No birth or death dates are provided for any person in the source. No research blockers remain.

itemChecks.reason: The source text 惠懷之際 in s0012 refers to the period of political and social turmoil during the late Western Jin, conventionally dated from the start of Emperor Hui's effective rule (290 AD, after Sima Lun's coup) to the end of Emperor Huai's reign (313 AD). The phrase literally means 'between Hui and Huai' but in Jin Shu usage it encompasses the entire period of the War of the Eight Princes and the Disaster of Yongjia. s0012 states that Hedong was the first to be disturbed during this period, and s0013 records Guo Pu's divination in direct response. The interval 290-313 is justified as the event-uncertainty window for when this turmoil—and thus Guo Pu's divination—could have occurred, not merely as an import of two whole reigns.

itemChecks.reason: The source phrase 終於建平太守 in s0006 uses the classical Chinese biographical formula 終於 + office title, which conventionally means 'died in office' rather than merely 'ended his career in office.' The word 終 implies the end of life, not just a career transition. In the Jin Shu's biographical convention, this formula is used specifically to record death while holding a post, distinguishing it from simple career enumeration. Thus s0006 provides explicit evidence that Guo Yuan died while serving as Grand Administrator of Jianping.
